note: Functions that tests/ replaces and no test executes for real, with the reason each
is acceptable. Read by tools/check_patched_guarantees.py, whose docstring says what
the check is for and why its evidence is collected at runtime.
An entry says: every test that mentions this function substitutes something else
for it, nothing in the suite runs it, and that is the right arrangement for this
particular function. It is not a note. It is a claim someone has to be able to
disagree with later, which is what the `why` requirement is about.
Rules the checker enforces on this file, so they cannot be quietly relaxed:
- `file` and `function` both. An entry keyed on a bare name would exempt every
first-party definition of that name, including ones added after the entry. The
lesson of data/acquire/*.sh, in tools/screen_allowlist.json: an entry keyed on
anything broader than the thing itself stops naming what it permits.
- A `why` of at least eight words. Crude, and it still catches 'flaky' and 'N/A'.
- No stale entries. An entry naming something that is not a candidate — not
patched anywhere, or no longer defined in that file — fails the run rather than
being ignored, because an exemption that outlives its function becomes an
exemption for whatever takes the name next.
The list is empty, and that is the intended steady state rather than an accident.
The one candidate the check found on its first run was src/eval/run_sealed_eval.py's
_loader_for, and the answer was to write the test that exercises its refusal branch
(tests/test_seal_internals.py::test_an_unknown_corpus_has_no_loader) rather than to
write an entry here. That is the order to keep: an entry is what you add when
running the real function is genuinely impossible, not when it is inconvenient.
